finding.claim: The LFS batch 'download' operation never validates the attacker-supplied oid before using it to build a filesystem path. _is_valid_oid is enforced only in handle_download, handle_upload and handle_verify, not in the batch handler. An unauthenticated client can therefore probe whether arbitrary files exist on the server. The oid is split by position, so '../../../../etc/passwd' gives sha[0:2]='..' and sha[2:4]='/.'. The second piece is absolute, so os.path.join discards the earlier components and the result resolves to /etc/passwd. A 'download' action is returned for an existing file and a 404 error otherwise, which makes an existence oracle. File contents are not readable this way, because the GET download path re-validates the oid. For 'upload', unvalidated oids are reflected into hrefs, but later requests validate them. The href also embeds the unvalidated Host header.
finding.source: JSON body of POST batch request: objects[].oid (attacker-controlled string, no format check), line 120

trace.note: oid = obj.get('oid') taken from request JSON; only a truthiness check on line 123, no _is_valid_oid call
self._object_exists(oid) is called with the unvalidated oid
os.path.join(self.path,'objects',sha[0:2],sha[2:4],sha) is built with no sanitisation; a '/'-leading sha[2:4] makes the join absolute
open(path,'rb') succeeds for any existing readable file; FileNotFoundError is mapped to KeyError, so the response reveals whether the file exists

finding.guards_checked: _is_valid_oid (lfs_server.py:46) is applied in handle_download (173), handle_upload (198) and handle_verify (242) but not in the batch handler (119-160). LFSStore._sha_path has no validation. No authentication exists on the server. In web.py, the dumb-HTTP routes restrict paths with strict regexes ([0-9a-f]{2}/[0-9a-f]{38}, \w+-<hex>.pack), so no traversal there.
